speaker: Chris Olah
title: What the hell is going on inside neural networks? | Chris Olah
question: Why do external or siloed AI safety teams typically fall a year or more behind the frontier compared to teams tightly integrated with large-model scaling efforts?
guest: It depends a lot on the exact institutional setup. If you're at a company that's training large models but aren't closely integrated with the scaling efforts in particular, you might still be looking at a six-month to one-year delay. That's due to the need for specialized infrastructure for working with these models, the fact that these models cost a lot to do anything with—just like they cost a lot to train—the fact that operational expertise may only reside with the people training them so you don't know how to work with them, and the fact that it's really hard to integrate with a project while it's actively being worked on. You end up waiting for the model to be polished and handed out, and you probably need engineers who have expertise working with large models to help build the tooling you need to do useful work on top of them. On the other extreme, if you're at an academic lab, that gap is growing dramatically—many academic labs only have a couple GPUs and lack expertise training even moderately large models, so they're working far behind the state of the art.

points.note: Accept: difficulty plugging into live, fast-moving training projects mid-flight, forcing external or siloed groups to wait for polished releases. Do not credit: generic complaints about corporate bureaucracy or slow peer review.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The main reason is access: the most informative safety work depends on the newest, largest models, and those exist only inside the labs that are scaling them. External or siloed teams usually work with models that are public or released to them, which tend to trail internal systems by months to a year or more. Their findings therefore describe behaviours and failure modes of the previous generation.

Several other gaps compound this:

- **Depth of access.** Interpretability, fine-tuning and training-time interventions need weights, activations, training data and checkpoints, whereas outsiders often get only API access.
- **Compute and infrastructure.** Running experiments at frontier scale takes clusters and engineering tooling that few outside groups can afford or replicate.
- **Tacit knowledge.** Much of what matters about how large models are trained, and how they behave, is unpublished and spreads through daily contact with the scaling teams.
- **Feedback loops.** Integrated teams see new capabilities as they emerge and can adjust their research agenda, and influence training and deployment, before release rather than after.

This view originates largely from Anthropic's "Core Views on AI Safety" argument, and critics note it also conveniently justifies building frontier models.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
External and siloed AI safety teams fall behind because frontier safety is an empirical discipline tightly coupled to scale, proprietary infrastructure, and live training dynamics. External researchers mostly rely on open-weight models—which lag leading closed systems by roughly a year—or restricted post-deployment APIs that conceal weights, activations, training data, and intermediate checkpoints. Even internally siloed teams often receive static models late in the release cycle rather than participating directly in pre-training and reinforcement learning runs.

This access gap is decisive because critical failure modes—such as reward hacking, scheming, sycophancy, and complex agentic behaviors—frequently emerge only at frontier scale or under new training regimes like large-scale reinforcement learning and inference-time compute scaling, causing mitigations validated on smaller or older models to break down. Meanwhile, scaling teams rapidly iterate on unpublished architectures, data mixtures, and distributed engineering stacks. Without shared compute, white-box tooling, and the tacit day-to-day knowledge of scaling engineers, isolated safety teams cannot co-design and test interventions inside live training runs, leaving them perpetually reacting to yesterday’s paradigms.

noweb.answer: External and siloed AI safety teams lag behind the frontier primarily due to delayed model access, scale-dependent phenomena, and disconnected infrastructure. Frontier capabilities and their sharpest failure modes—such as sophisticated reward hacking, sandbagging, or deceptive reasoning—emerge unpredictably at massive scale and within novel post-training paradigms. Because external researchers must rely on smaller open-weight models or delayed, black-box API releases, they end up studying older capability regimes, often finding that alignment techniques validated at small scale fail to transfer to frontier systems. Even internal safety teams, when siloed, miss the tacit, fast-moving details of data mixtures, training recipes, and reinforcement learning environments that shape model behavior months before a final checkpoint exists or becomes publicly visible. By contrast, tightly integrated safety teams share compute clusters, production tooling, and immediate feedback loops with scaling researchers. With real-time access to weights, activations, training data, and intermediate checkpoints, embedded teams can diagnose emerging risks during live runs and co-design interventions alongside capability advances, rather than retrofitting defenses long after critical training decisions are locked in.

models.answer: External or siloed AI safety teams fall behind primarily because they lack timely, deep access to frontier models and the infrastructure required to study them. Frontier labs train and iterate on new architectures, post-training methods, and agentic scaffolds internally for months before any public release, meaning outside researchers typically only see a generation of models after capabilities teams have already moved on. Even when access is granted, it is often restricted to black-box APIs rather than the model weights, internal activations, training data, and intermediate checkpoints needed for interpretability, fine-tuning, and alignment research. Furthermore, many safety techniques and emergent failure modes only manifest at frontier scale, which requires massive compute and specialized engineering stacks that independent groups rarely possess. Finally, tightly integrated teams benefit from continuous feedback loops and unpublished tacit knowledge about how training dynamics are shifting, whereas siloed teams must infer those changes indirectly and risk building safeguards for yesterday's problems.

noweb.answer: External or siloed AI safety teams fall behind primarily because they lack timely access to frontier models, compute, and internal research context. By the time a frontier model is publicly released, leading labs are often already training its successor, and external researchers typically get only black-box API access rather than model weights, activations, or intermediate training checkpoints. Without shared large-scale compute clusters and post-training infrastructure, siloed groups cannot test alignment, interpretability, or red-teaming interventions at the scales where new capabilities and failure modes actually emerge. Equally important is tacit knowledge: frontier scaling involves constant, undocumented shifts in architectures, data mixtures, and reinforcement learning recipes. Teams embedded directly within scaling efforts see these changes as they happen and can iterate on mitigations inside the training loop, whereas isolated teams are forced to study outdated paradigms months later through public releases and delayed papers.
